title: KidsCoin Family Learning Expansion 2 · Twenty-Question Edition
description: Eighty-four additional family-planning questions, fourteen for each open KidsCoin lesson, bringing every lesson to twenty questions when merged with the six recovered base questions.

earn-before-spend.prompt: Which action should happen before Family KC is added for a chore?
options: A parent approves the completed chore
earn-before-spend.explanation: A completed chore waits for a parent decision before fictional Family KC is awarded.

earn-before-spend.prompt: Why might a parent reject a completed-chore request?
options: The chore may need to be finished or checked again
The app requires a credit card
earn-before-spend.explanation: A parent may ask for the chore to be completed or checked again before approval.

earn-before-spend.prompt: What is a fair way to earn toward a larger family reward?
options: Complete several agreed chores or lessons over time
Change the balance with browser tools
earn-before-spend.explanation: Several approved efforts can build a fictional balance gradually and fairly.

earn-before-spend.prompt: Which statement best describes earning in KidsCoin?
options: It practices responsibility with fictional points
It sends money outside the family
earn-before-spend.explanation: KidsCoin is a family practice system using fictional points, not wages or real payments.

earn-before-spend.prompt: A chore is marked done but has not been checked yet. What happens next?
earn-before-spend.explanation: KidsCoin waits for a parent to approve a completed chore before adding fictional Family KC.

earn-before-spend.prompt: Why is it useful to agree on a chore before doing it for KC?
options: Everyone knows the task and reward ahead of time
It makes every chore worth the same
earn-before-spend.explanation: Clear expectations help everyone understand what needs to be done and what fictional reward is attached.

earn-before-spend.prompt: You earn 3 KC for one approved task and 6 KC for another. How much did you earn?
Which is a responsible way to build a KC balance?
options: Complete agreed tasks and lessons over time
earn-before-spend.explanation: A fair balance grows from the activities the family agreed on, not from bypassing the rules.

earn-before-spend.prompt: Why might two chores have different KC rewards?
options: They may take different effort or responsibility
The app changes prices every minute
One belongs to a public market
earn-before-spend.explanation: Families can choose different fictional rewards for tasks that require different time, effort, or responsibility.

earn-before-spend.prompt: A task earns 9 KC and 18 XP. What does the XP help track?
earn-before-spend.explanation: XP is another fictional progress measure inside the app and does not have cash value.

earn-before-spend.prompt: What should happen if a chore needs to be redone?
options: Finish it properly and ask for approval again
earn-before-spend.explanation: Redoing the task and asking for approval again keeps the family agreement fair and clear.

earn-before-spend.prompt: Which choice shows earning before spending?
options: Complete an agreed task, receive approval, then consider a reward
Request a reward before checking the balance
earn-before-spend.explanation: The sequence is effort, approval, earning, and then deciding whether to save or request a reward.

earn-before-spend.prompt: You have 12 KC and earn 9 KC. What is your new balance before any reward is redeemed?
What is the main lesson behind earn-before-spend?
options: Build resources through agreed effort before using them
Every task should lead to a purchase
earn-before-spend.explanation: Earning first practices planning and responsibility before choosing how to use a fictional balance.

needs-and-wants.prompt: Which choice is usually a need for school?
needs-and-wants.explanation: Required basic supplies help a student participate, while the other choices are usually extras.

needs-and-wants.prompt: A family has enough KC for one choice. Which should come first?
needs-and-wants.explanation: Important agreed needs should generally be considered before optional extras.

needs-and-wants.prompt: Can the same item be a need for one person and a want for another?
options: No, every item has one permanent category
needs-and-wants.explanation: Circumstances matter; an item may be necessary for one person and optional for another.

needs-and-wants.prompt: What question helps separate a need from a want?
options: Is this necessary for safety, health, or an important daily responsibility?
needs-and-wants.explanation: Thinking about safety, health, and important responsibilities helps identify needs.

needs-and-wants.prompt: Which choice is most likely a need on a rainy school day?
options: A safe rain jacket you already planned for
needs-and-wants.explanation: A rain jacket can meet a practical daily need, while the other choices are usually optional extras.

needs-and-wants.prompt: Why should needs usually be planned before wants?
options: Needs support important daily life and responsibilities
needs-and-wants.explanation: Planning for important needs first helps protect the things required for daily life before optional extras.

needs-and-wants.prompt: A working water bottle is lost before school. Is replacing it more likely a need or a want?
needs-and-wants.explanation: If the bottle is needed for the school day, replacing it can be a practical need.

needs-and-wants.prompt: You already have a working backpack but like a new design. The new one is usually what?
needs-and-wants.explanation: When the current item still works, a different style is usually an optional want.

needs-and-wants.prompt: What can help when two family members disagree about whether something is a need?
options: Explain the reason and listen to each person's situation
needs-and-wants.explanation: Needs depend on circumstances, so sharing reasons and listening helps the family make a thoughtful decision.

needs-and-wants.prompt: Which plan leaves room for both needs and wants?
options: Cover important needs, save some, then choose an affordable extra
needs-and-wants.explanation: A balanced plan can cover important needs, protect savings, and still include an affordable want.

needs-and-wants.prompt: A required school project needs poster board. What is poster board in this situation?
needs-and-wants.explanation: Because it is required to complete an important school responsibility, it functions as a need in this situation.

needs-and-wants.prompt: Which question best checks whether a purchase is a want?
options: Could I safely wait or use what I already have?
needs-and-wants.explanation: If you can safely wait or use something you already have, the new item may be an optional want.

needs-and-wants.prompt: Why can a want still be worth planning for?
options: Fun and personal goals can matter after important needs are covered
needs-and-wants.explanation: Optional goals can bring enjoyment and motivation, especially when they fit after needs and savings.

needs-and-wants.prompt: What is the strongest needs-and-wants habit?
options: Pause, identify the purpose, and decide what matters first
needs-and-wants.explanation: Thinking about purpose and priority leads to better choices than using a label automatically.

saving-goal.prompt: You have 21 KC and save 3 more. What is the new balance?
A reward costs 54 KC. You have 36 KC. How much more is needed?
Which plan reaches a 45 KC goal from 18 KC?
saving-goal.explanation: Three rewards of 9 KC add 27 KC; 18 + 27 = 45.

saving-goal.prompt: Why can a written KC goal help?
options: It makes the target and progress easier to track
saving-goal.explanation: A clear written goal helps an explorer compare the current balance with the target.

saving-goal.prompt: You have 30 KC and want 45 KC. How much more do you need?
If you save 6 KC from each approved activity, how many activities add 18 KC?
saving-goal.explanation: Three groups of 6 KC equal 18 KC.

saving-goal.prompt: Which saving goal is easiest to measure?
saving-goal.explanation: A specific amount and purpose make progress easy to measure.

saving-goal.prompt: You have 33 KC and earn 3 KC. Which goal have you reached?
What can help protect a saving goal when a small want appears?
options: Compare the want with the goal before spending
saving-goal.explanation: Comparing the short-term want with the larger goal helps you decide which matters more.

saving-goal.prompt: A goal costs 72 KC. You have 45 KC. What fraction of the goal remains as 27 KC?
saving-goal.explanation: Twenty-seven is less than half of 72, so you have already saved more than half.

saving-goal.prompt: Why is checking the ledger useful while saving?
options: It shows where the balance changed
saving-goal.explanation: The ledger helps you understand earnings and redemptions that move the fictional balance.

saving-goal.prompt: You save 9 KC, then 6 KC, then 3 KC. How much did you add altogether?
saving-goal.explanation: Nine plus six plus three equals 18 KC.

saving-goal.prompt: What is a useful response if a saving goal will take longer than expected?
options: Adjust the plan and keep tracking progress
saving-goal.explanation: A realistic plan can be adjusted when progress is slower than expected without abandoning the goal.

options: Choosing to keep some resources now for a later goal
saving-goal.explanation: Saving means intentionally keeping part of what you have so it can support a future goal.

read-the-ledger.prompt: The ledger shows +6 KC and then -3 KC. What is the overall change?
read-the-ledger.explanation: Adding 6 and subtracting 3 leaves a net increase of 3 KC.

read-the-ledger.prompt: Which ledger detail tells when an entry happened?
read-the-ledger.explanation: The timestamp records the date and time of the local ledger entry.

read-the-ledger.prompt: Why should a rejected request not subtract KC?
options: No reward was approved or redeemed
read-the-ledger.explanation: KC is only deducted when a reward redemption is actually approved.

read-the-ledger.prompt: A balance seems wrong. What is the best first check?
options: Review recent earn and spend entries with a parent
read-the-ledger.explanation: Recent ledger entries usually explain how the local fictional balance changed.

read-the-ledger.prompt: The ledger shows +9 KC, +3 KC, and -6 KC. What is the net change?
read-the-ledger.explanation: Nine plus three minus six equals a net increase of 6 KC.

read-the-ledger.prompt: Why is the newest ledger entry often checked first?
options: It may explain the most recent balance change
read-the-ledger.explanation: A recent entry is a good first place to look when you are trying to explain a recent change.

read-the-ledger.prompt: A +3 KC entry is followed by +6 KC. What do both entries represent?
read-the-ledger.explanation: Positive KC entries represent fictional earnings that increase the local balance.

read-the-ledger.prompt: What should a clear ledger label tell you?
read-the-ledger.explanation: A useful label makes it easy to connect an entry with the task, lesson, or approved reward that caused it.

read-the-ledger.prompt: Your balance was 42 KC and the ledger shows -27 KC. What balance remains?
Why should ledger entries stay in order by time?
options: It helps reconstruct how the balance changed
read-the-ledger.explanation: A time-ordered history makes it easier to follow the sequence of earnings and redemptions.

read-the-ledger.prompt: Which entry would increase the balance?
read-the-ledger.explanation: A positive approved earning increases the balance; a redemption decreases it.

read-the-ledger.prompt: If the ledger and balance do not seem to match, what is a careful next step?
options: Review the entries with a parent before changing anything
read-the-ledger.explanation: Checking the recorded entries together is safer than guessing or deleting the history.

read-the-ledger.prompt: What makes a ledger useful for planning?
options: It shows patterns in earning and redeeming
read-the-ledger.explanation: Seeing how often resources come in and go out can help with realistic goals.

read-the-ledger.prompt: Which sentence best summarizes a ledger?
read-the-ledger.explanation: A ledger records events that add to or subtract from a balance.

plan-a-reward.prompt: You have 48 KC. Which reward can you request right now?
plan-a-reward.explanation: Forty-eight KC is enough for a 45 KC reward but not the higher-cost choices.

plan-a-reward.prompt: What happens to the balance while a reward request is pending?
options: It stays unchanged until a parent decides
plan-a-reward.explanation: Pending requests do not deduct Family KC before parent approval.

plan-a-reward.prompt: Two rewards cost 27 KC and 45 KC. How much KC would both cost together?
Why might a parent approve a reward for a different day?
options: The timing may need to fit the family schedule
The KC has a market price
The reward belongs to a stranger
plan-a-reward.explanation: A family reward can be approved while its timing is planned around real family needs.

plan-a-reward.prompt: You have 54 KC. Which listed reward cost can you fully cover?
plan-a-reward.explanation: A 54 KC balance can fully cover a reward that costs 54 KC.

plan-a-reward.prompt: You want a 72 KC reward and have 60 KC. How much more is needed?
Why compare two reward costs before requesting one?
options: To see which fits your balance and goal better
plan-a-reward.explanation: Comparing costs helps you choose a reward that fits your current balance and priorities.

plan-a-reward.prompt: What should you consider besides KC cost when planning a family reward?
options: Whether the timing works for the family
plan-a-reward.explanation: Family rewards can depend on schedules, availability, and parent approval as well as the fictional KC cost.

plan-a-reward.prompt: You have 81 KC and choose a 45 KC reward. What balance would remain after approval?
Which plan keeps a future goal alive after a reward?
options: Check what balance will remain before requesting
plan-a-reward.explanation: Looking at the remaining balance helps you decide whether the reward fits alongside another goal.

plan-a-reward.prompt: A reward request is pending. What is the best assumption?
options: Wait for the parent decision before treating it as approved
plan-a-reward.explanation: Pending means the family decision has not been made yet, so the reward should not be treated as approved.

plan-a-reward.prompt: Why can a smaller reward sometimes be the better choice?
options: It may fit the balance while preserving savings for another goal
plan-a-reward.explanation: A lower-cost option can meet a goal while leaving more of the fictional balance for future plans.

plan-a-reward.prompt: Which sequence is best for a reward plan?
options: Choose a goal, check cost, save, request, wait for approval
Hide the goal, guess the cost, spend
plan-a-reward.explanation: A clear sequence keeps the goal, cost, saving, and parent decision connected.

plan-a-reward.prompt: What does a good reward plan balance?
options: What you want, what you have, and what the family can approve
plan-a-reward.explanation: Good planning connects personal goals with the available fictional balance and the family's real schedule and rules.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Where can another family see your KidsCoin notes?
options: Nowhere; notes stay in this browser
family-kc-boundary.explanation: KidsCoin notes are device-local and are not posted for other families.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: What could clearing this browser's local data do?
family-kc-boundary.explanation: Because the data is local, clearing browser storage can remove KidsCoin progress unless it was backed up.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: What is the safest description of the parent PIN?
options: A convenience lock against casual taps
family-kc-boundary.explanation: The local PIN is a convenience boundary and is not strong account security.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Why does KidsCoin avoid real-money purchases?
options: The app is designed for private family learning with fictional rewards
Real money makes every lesson easier
Purchases are required for local storage
family-kc-boundary.explanation: The system practices planning and responsibility without payments, sales, or financial accounts.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Does Family KC have a dollar exchange rate?
family-kc-boundary.explanation: Family KC is fictional and has no cash exchange rate.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Who controls family reward approvals in KidsCoin?
options: The parent or caregiver using Parent Mode
family-kc-boundary.explanation: Reward approvals stay inside the family's Parent Mode rather than going to an outside service.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: What does device-local mean for KidsCoin data?
options: It is stored in this browser unless you export or clear it
It is stored at a bank
family-kc-boundary.explanation: Device-local data stays in this browser instead of automatically syncing to an outside account.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Why should the parent PIN not be treated like strong security?
options: It is only a local convenience lock
family-kc-boundary.explanation: The PIN helps prevent casual taps but is not designed as strong account authentication.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: What happens if Family KC is never redeemed?
options: It simply remains a fictional local balance
family-kc-boundary.explanation: Family KC remains a fictional number in the local family app until the family uses it for an approved reward.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Does KidsCoin sell items inside the app?
family-kc-boundary.explanation: KidsCoin has no purchases; its rewards are family-planned and parent approved.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: What is a safe way to think about Family KC?
family-kc-boundary.explanation: Family KC is a pretend planning and responsibility tool, not real money or a financial product.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Can another player transfer Family KC into your profile over the internet?
family-kc-boundary.explanation: There is no online transfer system; KidsCoin is a private device-local family experience.

family-kc-boundary.prompt: Why is it important to know the difference between fictional KC and real money?
options: Real money has real-world value and responsibilities; Family KC does not
KC can always be cashed out
Real money is only used in games
family-kc-boundary.explanation: Keeping the boundary clear prevents a practice system from being confused with real financial accounts or purchases.

options: Learn and plan with pretend rewards, no ads or purchases
family-kc-boundary.explanation: KidsCoin is designed for private family learning with fictional rewards and no ads, purchases, or financial products.

review.note: Family-planning practice questions with no real-money, investment, banking, or cryptocurrency instruction.
